buildUp: Start with the fuel: a thin gas of deuterium and tritium heated to around 150 million °C, which turns it into a plasma that would destroy any wall it touched.
Charged particles follow magnetic field lines, so eighteen D-shaped coils wrap the long way round a doughnut-shaped vessel, making a field with no ends for the plasma to leak out of.

A ring-shaped field alone lets the plasma drift outwards, so a central solenoid drives millions of amps through the plasma, twisting the field into a helix, and ring coils outside hold the plasma's position and D shape.

Copper coils that strong would burn enormous power, so the magnets are superconducting at about -269 °C, which means a vacuum cryostat and a thermal shield to keep heat away from them only a few metres from the plasma.
Neutrons escape the magnetic cage, so the vessel is lined with blanket modules that stop them, turning their energy into heat and shielding the magnets behind.
Heat and helium ash leaking from the plasma's edge have to go somewhere, so the field is shaped to steer them onto a heavily armoured divertor at the bottom, where pumps draw off the exhaust.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Hold the fuel with magnetism instead of walls. Heated that much, the fuel becomes a plasma of charged particles, and charged particles can't easily cross magnetic field lines, so a field shaped into a twisted doughnut keeps the plasma away from every surface. Superconducting magnets make that field without wasting power, and the neutrons that escape the cage carry the energy out to be turned into heat.

hardParts.title: The hottest surface in the machine
hardParts.why: Everything that leaks out of the plasma edge is funnelled onto a narrow ring of the divertor, at up to about 10 MW on every square metre, a few thousand kettles' worth of power on a patch the size of a table top. Its tungsten armour and water cooling must take that for years while being bombarded by particles and neutrons, and still be swapped out by robots.

hardParts.title: The coldest things next to the hottest
hardParts.why: Superconducting magnets at about -269 °C sit only a few metres from plasma at 150 million °C, with neutrons and heat trying to reach them. They also feel enormous magnetic forces trying to burst them outwards and crush them inwards, so each must be immensely strong as well as cold, and the cryostat, thermal shield and vessel shielding all exist largely to protect them.

hardParts.title: Keeping an unstable plasma in place
hardParts.why: A plasma stretched into a tall D shape holds more pressure but is naturally unstable up and down, and would hit the wall within a fraction of a second if left alone. Sensors and feedback adjust the outer coils within milliseconds, and if the plasma current collapses suddenly anyway, the vessel must survive huge electromagnetic forces.

principles.explanation: A helium nucleus weighs slightly less than the deuterium and tritium that fuse to make it, and that missing mass, about 0.4 percent, comes out as energy, by Einstein's E = mc². Because c squared is so enormous, each reaction releases millions of times more energy than a chemical reaction like burning, which only rearranges electrons. Kilogram for kilogram, fusion fuel holds several million times more energy than coal or gas. About 80 percent of it leaves on a fast neutron, the rest on the helium nucleus.
principles.title: A little mass becomes a lot of energy

principles.explanation: Positive nuclei repel each other, so they only fuse if they collide at huge speeds, which is why the fuel has to be heated to around 150 million °C. Two positive nuclei push each other away harder and harder as they get closer, but if they get close enough, roughly the width of a nucleus, the much stronger nuclear force grabs them and they fuse. At the atomic scale temperature is speed: the hotter the fuel, the faster its nuclei fly. At that temperature, enough of the fastest particles get through, helped by quantum tunnelling, which lets them occasionally slip through the barrier rather than climbing all the way over it. Deuterium and tritium are used because they fuse far more easily than any other pair.
principles.title: Beating the electrical repulsion

principles.explanation: Charged particles spiral round magnetic field lines instead of crossing them, so a field bent into a ring and gently twisted can hold the plasma away from every wall. A magnetic field pushes a moving charged particle sideways, so it spirals tightly round the field lines, like a bead on a wire. A straight tube of field would leak out at its ends, so you bend it round into a ring with no ends. But a bent field is stronger on the inside of the curve than the outside, which makes particles slowly drift across it; twisting the field lines into a gentle helix, by running a current through the plasma itself, cancels that drift out on average.
principles.title: Charged particles follow magnetic field lines

principles.explanation: Gain needs a plasma that is hot, dense and holds its heat long enough, and bigger plasmas hold heat longer, a big reason tokamaks aimed at gain are so large. A plasma only gives out more energy than you put in when all three are met, and what matters is roughly the three multiplied together. A plasma loses heat through its surface but makes fusion throughout its volume, so like a big pot of soup that stays hot longer than a small cup, a bigger machine holds its heat for longer. This one aims to make about 500 MW of fusion power from about 50 MW of heating.
principles.title: Gain needs heat, density and time

firstPrinciples.problem: Get energy the way the Sun does, by fusing light atoms into heavier ones, using fuel drawn from seawater and lithium, with no carbon dioxide and no long chain reaction to run away. The catch is that atomic nuclei are all positively charged and repel each other fiercely, so they only fuse if they slam together at tremendous speed, which means a fuel heated to over a hundred million degrees. Nothing solid can hold something that hot, and the fuel has to be kept hot and dense for long enough that it gives out more energy than it took to heat.

questions.answer: The plasma is extremely thin, so it holds surprisingly little heat in total, and the magnetic field keeps it off the walls. The heat that does leak out is steered onto the cooled divertor, and the neutrons' energy is caught in the water-cooled blanket.
questions.question: Why doesn't the plasma at 150 million °C melt the steel vessel a few metres away?

questions.answer: Magnetic fields only push on charged particles, and neutrons have no charge. They fly straight out of the plasma, which is useful, because that is how the energy is carried to where it can be collected as heat.
questions.question: Why do the neutrons end up in the blanket rather than being held by the magnetic field like the rest of the plasma?

questions.answer: The plasma current is driven like a transformer, by steadily ramping the current in the central solenoid. That can only keep ramping so far before it reaches its limit, so each pulse has to end and the solenoid be reset.
questions.question: Why does this tokamak run in pulses of a few minutes rather than continuously?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The remarkable idea is that a gas hotter than the centre of the Sun can be held in place by nothing but invisible field lines, with the coldest things on Earth a few metres away. The plasma itself is surprisingly thin, closer to a vacuum than to air, so the cage holds very little actual material; that is also why fusion can't run away like fission: if anything goes wrong the plasma simply cools and stops within seconds.

name: Fusion Reactor
overview:
A fusion reactor tries to do what the Sun does: squeeze light atoms together so hard that they fuse into heavier ones and release enormous amounts of energy. On Earth that means heating a thin gas of hydrogen isotopes, deuterium and tritium, to around 150 million °C, ten times hotter than the centre of the Sun. At that temperature the gas becomes a plasma, and no material wall could touch it without being destroyed, so the plasma has to be held in place by magnetic fields instead.

A tokamak does this with a doughnut-shaped magnetic cage. Eighteen huge D-shaped coils wrapped round the doughnut make a field that runs the long way round it. A tall central solenoid in the hole of the doughnut drives a strong current through the plasma itself, which twists the field into a helix, and ring-shaped coils outside shape and steady the plasma. The magnets are superconducting, so they are cooled to about -269 °C, only a few metres from the hottest plasma in the solar system.

The fusion reactions release fast neutrons that fly straight out through the magnetic cage and into the blanket lining the vessel, heating it; in a power station that heat would make steam to drive turbines. Exhaust and heat from the plasma edge are steered down onto the divertor at the bottom, the hardest-working surface in the machine. The whole thing sits inside the cryostat, a giant steel vacuum flask about 30 m tall.

parts.description: Eighteen giant D-shaped superconducting coils that wrap round the doughnut and make the main magnetic field.

details.didYouKnow: On ITER, nineteen of these coils were built, not eighteen: the extra one is a spare, made in case a coil is damaged, because winding a replacement from scratch would take years.
details.howItWorks: A huge current flows round each coil, and together the eighteen make a magnetic field that runs the long way round the doughnut. Charged particles in the plasma spiral tightly along field lines rather than crossing them, so the field acts like invisible rails keeping the hot gas off the walls. The D shape is deliberate: the magnetic forces try to burst each coil outwards, and a D lets the coil carry that load mostly as tension instead of bending.
keyNumbers: About 17 m tall and roughly 360 tonnes each
Up to about 11.8 T at the conductor
Roughly 68,000 amps in each coil
details.madeOf: Niobium-tin superconducting strands twisted into cables inside steel jackets, with supercritical helium flowing through to hold them at about 4 K, and each winding is clamped inside a massive stainless-steel case. Niobium-tin keeps superconducting in the very strong fields these coils make, where cheaper niobium-titanium would not.

parts.name: Toroidal field coils

parts.description: Steel shear panels bridging neighbouring D coils above and below the vessel, so the ring of coils can't twist over.

details.didYouKnow: The joints between panels are built to slip very slightly under load rather than stay perfectly rigid. A little give spreads the force and stops any one bolt taking too much of it.
details.howItWorks: When the plasma current runs through the field of the D coils, each coil feels a sideways force that tries to tip it over like a falling domino. These panels tie each coil to its neighbours, so the eighteen brace one another and the forces cancel round the ring. They sit above and below the vessel, in the gaps between the ports.
keyNumbers: One set between each pair of the 18 coils
Kept at about 4 K, like the coils
Must carry large forces that reverse with each pulse
details.madeOf: High-strength stainless steel castings or forgings bolted and keyed to the coil cases. They stay cold along with the coils, so the steel has to remain tough at about 4 K.

parts.name: Inter-coil structures

parts.description: Tall stack of superconducting coils in the doughnut's hole that drives a huge current through the plasma itself.

details.didYouKnow: ITER's central solenoid modules were made by General Atomics in the United States and shipped across the Atlantic one by one. The magnetic forces inside are so strong that the stack has to be clamped together to stop the modules pushing apart.
details.howItWorks: The solenoid works like the first coil of a giant transformer, with the plasma ring as the second. As its current is ramped steadily, the changing magnetic field drives a current of millions of amps round the plasma, which heats it and twists the magnetic field into a helix that holds the plasma far more stably. Because the current can only ramp so far, a tokamak like this runs in pulses lasting minutes rather than continuously.
keyNumbers: About 18 m tall and about 1,000 tonnes
Peak field up to about 13 T
Drives a plasma current of about 15 million amps
Pulses of roughly 400 seconds
details.madeOf: Niobium-tin superconducting cable in steel jackets, wound into six independent modules stacked on top of each other and held together by a steel pre-compression structure. The modules can be driven separately, which helps shape the plasma as well as drive its current.

parts.name: Central solenoid

parts.description: Ring-shaped coil above the machine that helps shape the top of the plasma.

details.didYouKnow: ITER's topmost poloidal coil was built in Russia, in St Petersburg, and shipped to France, one of many parts of the machine made in member countries and assembled on site.
details.howItWorks: Poloidal field coils make a field that runs up and down, across the long way of the doughnut. This top coil, sitting close to the central solenoid, pulls and pushes on the upper part of the plasma current, stretching the plasma vertically and setting the shape of its top edge. A taller, D-shaped plasma holds more pressure for the same magnetic field, which makes fusion easier.
keyNumbers: Roughly 8 m across
Operates at about 4 K (-269 °C)
Field at the conductor up to about 6 T
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconducting cable in steel jackets, cooled to about 4 K by supercritical helium. Niobium-titanium is cheaper and easier to wind than niobium-tin and is good enough here, because the poloidal coils sit in weaker fields than the toroidal coils.

parts.name: Upper poloidal coil

parts.description: Ring coil over the shoulder of the D coils that shapes the upper outer flank of the plasma.

details.didYouKnow: The poloidal coils have to be threaded outside the D coils, so several of them must be lowered into place before the coils above can be fitted. The build order is planned around them.
details.howItWorks: This ring sits over the shoulder of the D coils and pulls on the plasma's upper outer flank. The poloidal coils act as a team, and adjusting the current in each one moves a different part of the plasma's edge, a little like tugging on strings round a balloon. Sensors feed a control system that keeps updating all the currents during a pulse.
keyNumbers: One of six main poloidal coils
Operates at about 4 K (-269 °C)
Tens of thousands of amps in the cable
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconducting cable in steel jackets, cooled to about 4 K by helium, wound flat in layers and wrapped in glass-fibre and resin insulation.

parts.name: Middle upper poloidal coil

parts.description: Large ring coil round the outside that pulls on the plasma to hold its D shape.

details.didYouKnow: ITER's largest poloidal field coils were too big to transport by road, so they were wound in a purpose-built factory on the ITER site itself.
details.howItWorks: A ring of current always tends to expand, like a stretched rubber band trying to fly apart, so the plasma constantly tries to push outwards. The field from the big outer coils crosses the plasma current and pushes the ring back in, holding it at the right radius. By adjusting the current in this coil, operators also pull out the upper outer corner of the plasma to give it its D shape.
keyNumbers: The largest poloidal coils are about 24 m across
Each weighs several hundred tonnes
Operates at about 4 K (-269 °C)
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconducting cable in steel jackets, wound flat in layers and sealed in insulation, then cooled to about 4 K. Niobium-titanium is ductile, so it can be wound into very large rings after the superconductor has been made.

parts.name: Outer upper poloidal coil

parts.description: Matching ring below that, with the others, keeps the plasma centred and steady.

details.didYouKnow: The outer coils are too slow on their own to catch the fastest vertical wobbles, because the thick steel vessel smooths out quick field changes, so ITER also has small extra coils mounted inside the vessel for fast control.
details.howItWorks: A plasma stretched tall like a D is naturally unstable up and down: left alone it would drift and slam into the top or bottom of the vessel within a fraction of a second. Sensors measure the plasma's position thousands of times a second, and a feedback system constantly adjusts the currents in the paired upper and lower outer coils to nudge it back to the centre. This coil also shapes the lower outer edge of the plasma.
keyNumbers: Ring roughly 17 to 24 m across
Operates at about 4 K (-269 °C)
Position corrections made within milliseconds
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconducting cable inside steel jackets, cooled to about 4 K and wrapped in layers of glass-fibre and resin insulation. It is mirrored by the upper outer coil, so the two can balance each other's pull on the plasma.

parts.name: Outer lower poloidal coil

parts.description: Ring coil under the shoulder of the D coils, working with its upper twin to steady the plasma.

details.didYouKnow: The lower coils must be put in position very early in construction, sitting waiting under the machine for years while everything else is built above them.
details.howItWorks: The lower twin of the middle upper coil. Together they hold the plasma's vertical stretch, and their currents can be pushed in opposite directions to nudge the whole plasma up or down. This coil also helps keep the X-point, and so the heat landing on the divertor, in the right place.
keyNumbers: One of six main poloidal coils
Operates at about 4 K (-269 °C)
Works in a pair with the upper coil
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconducting cable in steel jackets, cooled to about 4 K by helium, wound in flat layers and insulated with glass fibre and resin.

parts.name: Middle lower poloidal coil

parts.description: Ring coil under the machine that shapes the plasma's lower edge towards the divertor.

details.didYouKnow: ITER's lowest poloidal coil was built in China. It had to be put in place early, before most of the machine was assembled, because it sits beneath the rest of the machine and could not be fitted later.
details.howItWorks: This coil under the machine bends the magnetic field near the bottom of the plasma into a cross shape called an X-point. Beyond that point, field lines are opened up and steered down onto the divertor, so heat and particles escaping the plasma's edge land on armoured targets rather than on the main wall. Moving the current in this coil moves exactly where those strike points fall.
keyNumbers: Roughly 10 m across
Operates at about 4 K (-269 °C)
Field at the conductor up to about 6 T
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconducting cable in steel jackets, cooled to about 4 K by supercritical helium, inside a fibreglass and resin insulation wrap. Like the other poloidal coils, it is a flat ring wound from many turns of cable.

parts.name: Lower poloidal coil

parts.description: Insulated lines that carry current and liquid helium from outside the cryostat in to the cold coils.

details.didYouKnow: Copper leads conduct heat as well as current, so they can leak a lot of heat into the cold helium. Using a high-temperature superconductor for the cold part of the lead cuts that heat leak dramatically.
details.howItWorks: Every coil needs huge currents and a steady flow of liquid helium, but all of it has to come from the warm world outside. Each feeder is a vacuum-insulated line that carries superconducting busbars and helium pipes through the cryostat wall. At the outer end, current leads make the difficult step from room-temperature copper to the cold superconductor.
keyNumbers: Dozens of feeders on a machine this size
Busbars at about 4 K
Tens of thousands of amps per line
details.madeOf: Superconducting busbars and helium pipes nested inside a steel vacuum jacket with its own thermal shield. Current leads often use a high-temperature superconductor, which lets less heat leak down into the cold end.

parts.name: Magnet feeders

parts.description: Double-walled steel doughnut that holds the plasma in a near-perfect vacuum and is the first safety barrier.

details.didYouKnow: The word tokamak comes from a Russian acronym meaning toroidal chamber with magnetic coils. Soviet scientists developed the design in the 1950s and 60s, and its success made it the leading approach worldwide.
details.howItWorks: Pumps empty the vessel to an extremely high vacuum, so the plasma is not cooled or polluted by stray air. Water flows between its two steel walls to carry away heat, and shielding plates in that gap soak up neutrons to protect the magnets outside. The blanket, divertor and ports all hang on the vessel, so it also takes huge forces if the plasma current suddenly collapses.
keyNumbers: About 19 m across and 11 m tall
Roughly 5,000 tonnes
Built from 9 sectors welded together on site
details.madeOf: A special grade of low-cobalt stainless steel, welded as two walls with borated steel shielding plates between them. Stainless steel stays strong, can be welded leak-tight and copes well with neutrons, and keeping cobalt low reduces long-lived radioactivity.

parts.name: Vacuum vessel

parts.description: Hundreds of steel blocks faced with beryllium tiles lining the vessel, absorbing the neutrons and heat from the plasma.

details.didYouKnow: In a future power station the blanket would also make fuel: neutrons hitting lithium inside it would breed new tritium. ITER's main blanket does not, but special test blanket modules in its ports will try out designs that do.
details.howItWorks: Most of the energy from each fusion reaction is carried off by a fast neutron, which has no charge and so flies straight through the magnetic field. The neutrons smash into the blanket and slow down, turning their energy into heat that is carried away by cooling water. The blanket also shields the vessel and magnets behind it, and each module can be unbolted and replaced by remote-handling robots.
keyNumbers: About 440 modules
Each roughly 1 x 1.5 m and up to several tonnes
Lines roughly 600 m² of wall
Fast neutrons carry about 80 percent of the fusion energy
details.madeOf: Each module is a thick, water-cooled stainless-steel shield block with a first-wall panel bolted on the front: beryllium tiles bonded to a copper-alloy heat sink. Beryllium is a very light element, so atoms knocked off it do little to cool the plasma.

parts.name: Blanket modules

parts.description: Ring of cassettes along the bottom, armoured with tungsten, that takes the plasma's exhaust heat and helium ash.

details.didYouKnow: ITER originally planned to start with carbon-fibre targets, but in 2013 it switched to an all-tungsten divertor, partly because carbon would trap too much radioactive tritium.
details.howItWorks: The magnetic field near the bottom of the plasma is shaped so that the outer layer of field lines leads down onto the divertor's targets. Heat and particles that leak out of the plasma travel along those lines and land there, far from the main wall. Pumps beneath the cassettes draw off the helium ash left by fusion, along with unburnt fuel, so the plasma does not choke on its own waste.
keyNumbers: 54 cassettes in a ring
Heat loads up to about 10 MW/m², about 20 MW/m² briefly
Tungsten melts at about 3,400 °C
details.madeOf: Steel cassettes carrying water-cooled targets armoured with tungsten blocks. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal and is very hard to knock atoms off, so it survives where almost anything else would melt or erode.

parts.name: Divertor

parts.description: The fuel: a ring of deuterium and tritium gas heated to about 150 million °C, held off the walls by the magnets.

details.didYouKnow: Even though the plasma fills hundreds of cubic metres, it is so thin that the fuel inside at any moment weighs less than a gram, which is one reason a fusion reactor cannot run away like a fire.
details.howItWorks: At about 150 million °C, deuterium and tritium nuclei move fast enough to overcome their electrical repulsion and fuse, making a helium nucleus and a fast neutron. The helium stays trapped by the magnetic field and helps keep the plasma hot, while the neutrons escape to heat the blanket. Extra heating comes from beams of fast particles and from radio waves and microwaves, like a vast microwave oven.
keyNumbers: About 830 m³ in volume
Major radius about 6.2 m
Aims for about 500 MW of fusion from about 50 MW of heating
About 150 million °C
details.madeOf: A mix of deuterium, which is extracted from ordinary water, and tritium, a rare radioactive form of hydrogen that is made in nuclear reactors. At these temperatures the electrons are stripped from the atoms, leaving a soup of charged particles.

parts.name: Plasma

parts.description: Openings round the vessel's equator for heating beams, diagnostics, remote-handling arms and test blankets.

details.didYouKnow: ITER's neutral beams speed up particles to about a million electronvolts before neutralising them, so they can cross the magnetic field without being deflected and dump their energy deep in the plasma.
details.howItWorks: Ports are the vessel's doors to the outside world. Through them, neutral beam injectors fire fast particles into the plasma and antennas beam in radio waves and microwaves to heat it. Others carry diagnostics that measure temperature, density and shape, and some are used by remote-handling machines to reach inside. Each opening is filled with a heavy port plug that also blocks neutrons from escaping.
keyNumbers: About 44 openings on ITER in total
Upper, equatorial and lower levels
Around 50 diagnostic systems
details.madeOf: Stainless-steel ducts welded to the vacuum vessel, extending out through the cryostat wall. Port plugs are thick steel structures filled with shielding, built to be pulled out whole for servicing.

parts.name: Ports

parts.description: Sloping ducts from the top of the vessel, out between the coils, for microwave launchers and instruments.

details.didYouKnow: A microwave beam can be steered to a spot only a few centimetres across, to heat a thin ring of plasma and stop a growing magnetic wobble before it spreads.
details.howItWorks: These ducts slope up from the top of the vessel and pass out between the D coils and the poloidal rings. Some carry microwave launchers that steer narrow beams to precise spots in the plasma, used to heat it and to calm instabilities; others hold cameras and instruments. Each is closed by a removable plug.
keyNumbers: Around 18 on a machine this size
Several tonnes per port plug
Passes through three separate barriers
details.madeOf: Stainless-steel ducts welded to the vessel, with bellows where they cross the cold thermal shield and the cryostat wall so that they can move as the machine heats up.

parts.name: Upper ports

parts.description: Sloping ducts from under the vessel, used to pump out the exhaust and to carry divertor cassettes in and out.

details.didYouKnow: All 54 cassettes must be moved along rails inside the vessel to reach only a few doors, so the remote handling is planned like a very slow, very heavy sliding puzzle.
details.howItWorks: These ducts slope down from under the vessel, level with the divertor. The exhaust gas drawn from under the cassettes is pumped out through them. The largest also act as doors: a robot vehicle carries worn divertor cassettes out through the port, one at a time, because no person can enter once the machine is radioactive.
keyNumbers: Around 18 on a machine this size
Cassettes weigh about 10 tonnes each
Handled entirely by remote control
details.madeOf: Stainless-steel ducts welded to the vessel, with bellows for movement and thick shielding around the openings to keep neutrons from reaching the coils.

parts.name: Lower ports

parts.description: Building-sized particle accelerator that fires a beam of fast atoms through a port and into the plasma to heat it.

details.didYouKnow: Neutralising works much better with negative ions than positive ones at these energies, so large machines use negative ion sources, even though making them is far harder.
details.howItWorks: An ion source makes a stream of charged particles, and huge voltages accelerate them to very high speed. Charged particles would be turned back by the tokamak's magnets, so the beam first passes through a cell of gas that turns them back into neutral atoms. These fly straight through the field and into the plasma, where collisions share their energy and also help drive the plasma current.
keyNumbers: Around a million volts of acceleration
Tens of megawatts per beam line
Beam line tens of metres long in total
details.madeOf: A large steel vacuum tank holding the ion source, a stack of accelerating grids, a gas neutraliser and a water-cooled dump for leftover ions, all fed through a ceramic high-voltage bushing and pumped by cold panels.

parts.name: Neutral beam injector

parts.description: A gyrotron, a powerful microwave tube, feeding waveguides that beam its output in through an upper port.

details.didYouKnow: The seal between the gyrotron and the waveguide is often a window of synthetic diamond: few materials can pass a megawatt of microwaves without overheating and cracking.
details.howItWorks: A gyrotron whirls a beam of electrons round in a strong magnetic field, and they give up their energy as an intense microwave beam. Waveguides carry it into the machine. The frequency is picked to match the rate at which electrons circle the magnetic field in the plasma, so the energy is absorbed in a precise chosen spot, like a microwave oven with very good aim.
keyNumbers: About a megawatt from each gyrotron
Frequency of about 170 GHz
Pulses lasting many minutes
details.madeOf: A vacuum tube sitting inside a superconducting magnet, with a water-cooled copper collector on top to catch the spent electrons. The waveguides are precisely made corrugated metal tubes, and a diamond window seals the vacuum because diamond barely absorbs microwaves.

parts.name: Microwave heating line

parts.description: Cold pumps on the lower ports that freeze the exhaust gas out of the vessel, keeping its vacuum clean between pulses.

details.didYouKnow: Unburnt fuel is far more plentiful in the exhaust than helium ash, because only a small share of the fuel fuses on each pass. Most of what the pumps catch goes back into the machine.
details.howItWorks: A cryopump has no moving parts in contact with the gas. Panels chilled to a few kelvin make hydrogen and helium stick to them, so the gas is simply captured. After a while a valve closes and the panels warm up, releasing the gas to be sent off and recycled into new fuel, while another pump takes over.
keyNumbers: Six or so on the machine, on the lower ports
Panels at about 4 to 5 K
Regenerated in cycles of minutes
details.madeOf: Stainless-steel housings with panels coated in activated charcoal, cooled by supercritical helium. Charcoal's enormous surface traps even helium, which is almost impossible to freeze.

parts.name: Cryopumps

parts.description: Silver-coated steel shield cooled to about -190 °C that stops heat radiating onto the super-cold magnets.

details.didYouKnow: In 2022 cracks were found in cooling pipes on ITER's thermal shield, caused by corrosion, and the panels had to be repaired, one of the problems behind the machine's rescheduled start.
details.howItWorks: Even in a vacuum, warm objects radiate heat as infrared light, and the magnets at about 4 K would soak it up from the warm vessel and cryostat. The thermal shield sits between them and the magnets, intercepting that radiation at a much easier temperature. Helium gas flowing through pipes welded to its panels carries the heat away, so the expensive deep-cold cooling only has to deal with a small leftover.
keyNumbers: Kept at about 80 K (-193 °C)
Panels a couple of centimetres thick
Silver layer only a few micrometres thick
details.madeOf: Stainless-steel panels coated with a thin layer of silver. Polished silver gives off and absorbs very little infrared, so the shield both stays cool and passes on as little heat as possible.

parts.name: Thermal shield

parts.description: Giant stainless-steel vacuum flask round the whole machine, insulating the magnets from the warm building.

details.didYouKnow: It is the largest stainless-steel vacuum vessel ever built. Made in India, it arrived as dozens of segments that were welded into four huge sections in a workshop on the ITER site.
details.howItWorks: The cryostat works like a giant vacuum flask. Pumping the air out of it removes the gas that would otherwise carry heat from the warm building to the super-cold magnets. It also supports the weight of the whole tokamak on its base, and many pipes, cables and ports pass through its walls, each needing a vacuum-tight seal.
keyNumbers: About 29 m wide and 29 m tall
About 16,000 m³ inside
Roughly 3,800 tonnes
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, welded from thick plates. Stainless steel stays tough when cold, can be welded leak-tight on a huge scale and is not strongly magnetic, so it does not disturb the field.

parts.name: Cryostat

parts.description: Domed top of the cryostat, lifted off by crane during assembly and major maintenance.

details.didYouKnow: ITER's assembly hall has two overhead cranes that can work together to lift about 1,500 tonnes, enough for the heaviest pieces of the machine, including the cryostat sections.
details.howItWorks: The lid seals the top of the cryostat, completing the vacuum flask around the machine. It is the last big piece to go on, once everything inside is in place. It is domed rather than flat because a curved shape resists the push of the outside air on a vacuum far better than a flat plate of the same thickness.
keyNumbers: About 29 m across
Roughly 650 tonnes
Air presses on it with about 10 tonnes per square metre
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, like the rest of the cryostat, welded together from curved segments with ribs to stiffen it. Large flanges let it be bolted and sealed to the cylinder below.

parts.name: Cryostat lid

parts.description: A flexible steel leg under each D coil, carrying the magnets' weight while letting them shrink as they cool.

details.didYouKnow: A leg is a compromise between strength and heat: thick steel would carry the weight easily but pour heat into the coils. The flexible plates are as thin as the load allows.
details.howItWorks: The magnets weigh many thousands of tonnes and shrink noticeably when cooled from room temperature to about 4 K. These legs carry the weight but must also let the coils creep inward as they cool. Each has thin, flexible steel plates that bend sideways easily but are very stiff under compression.
keyNumbers: One under each of the 18 D coils
Coils shrink by a few centimetres as they cool
Carries the magnets' thousands of tonnes
details.madeOf: High-nickel steel plates bolted together in a stack, with cooled thermal anchors part-way along so little heat travels up the leg from the warm cryostat floor.

parts.name: Gravity supports

parts.description: Massive steel ring on the cryostat's floor that the whole machine stands on, passing its weight to the concrete below.

details.didYouKnow: A machine this large can be built on hundreds of steel-and-rubber bearings that let the whole building ride out an earthquake, instead of being fixed directly to the bedrock.
details.howItWorks: All the weight of the tokamak comes down through the legs onto this ring and on through the cryostat's base to the concrete floor. Spreading the load keeps the base from being crushed at each leg. In many designs, the floor below is also isolated from the ground to protect the machine during an earthquake.
keyNumbers: Carries a machine of many thousands of tonnes
Part of the cryostat's base
Set on the machine's main axis to within millimetres
details.madeOf: Very thick stainless-steel plate, welded into a large ring that forms part of the cryostat's base, with openings for pipes and for inspection.

parts.name: Pedestal ring

summary: A tokamak fusion reactor: a ring of plasma hotter than the Sun's core, held inside a doughnut-shaped steel vessel by giant superconducting magnets, all sealed in a huge vacuum flask called the cryostat.
